claim: A code-LLM-confidence empirical study evaluates 12 model checkpoints across 14 programming languages on a corpus explicitly constructed to exclude any project present in a major model's (LLaMA) training data, demonstrating explicit contamination control as an evaluation norm in this subarea.
stance_target: explicit contamination-control methodology is expected in rigorous code-LLM confidence studies
scope_conditions: code perplexity / intrinsic confidence measurement across languages, not calibration training
quoted_support: To avoid evaluation overfitting we synthesized the dataset of the analysis with code that is complementary to the code used to train LLaMA... we used the same dataset (snapshot 23 Feb 2023), and only kept (copyleft) GNU-licensed projects.

claim: Strongly-typed programming languages exhibit lower code perplexity (an intrinsic LLM confidence proxy) than dynamically-typed languages; Shell is universally high-perplexity and Java universally low across models tested.
stance_target: language-type effects on intrinsic code-LLM confidence
scope_conditions: 14 languages, 12 model checkpoints, GitHub-sourced code corpus
quoted_support: strongly-typed languages exhibit lower perplexity than dynamically typed languages... Shell appears universally high in perplexity, whereas Java appears low.
